implementation_notes: The presentation model is a plain class whose fields are JavaFX properties; the view binds widget properties to them (FXML binding expressions or addListener) and derived display state is expressed as bindings, so the enablement rule stays in the model. Invalidation and change listeners are the two notification granularities the binding API documents (lazy invalidation versus eager change), and bidirectional binding covers input controls. Because the model uses only javafx.beans types it can be constructed and tested without showing a stage; Swing has no equivalent, so on Swing the same model is a plain class with manual PropertyChangeListener wiring.
pitfalls: JavaFX is not thread-safe: model properties may only be read and written on the application thread, so background work must publish results through Platform.runLater (or a Task), not by writing properties directly.

bind() uses weak listeners for the bound property (the Property javadoc says so), but explicit addListener registrations are strong references - a view that adds listeners without removing them is never collected.
Bidirectional binding loops when both sides normalise or clamp values; bindBidirectional belongs only where the value is stored verbatim.

variants.name: Android ViewModel with LiveData observed by the view
variants.implementation_notes: On Android the framework answers the same need with the ViewModel: a screen-level state holder that survives configuration changes, exposes its state as LiveData, and is observed by the Activity or Fragment, where observation automatically unregisters when the view reaches the STOPPED state. The model holds the screen state and commands, the view renders it, and ViewModel.onCleared is the teardown hook. Choose this variant on Android; the JavaFX variant applies to desktop, and both keep the state holder free of view types so it can be tested with plain JUnit.
pitfalls: LiveData.observe must be called with a LifecycleOwner so the observer unregisters with the view; observeForever leaks until removeObservers is called.
setValue must run on the main thread (postValue for background threads), the same rule that applies to touching views.
A ViewModel must not hold Context, View or other lifecycle-related references: the Android documentation is explicit that the state holder can outlive its owner and such references leak.
